title: What not to put on the site for an accounting firm
metaTitle: Accounting firm website mistakes worth cutting
excerpt: Cut skylines and the word excellence from an accounting firm site. Keep who does the work, for whom, and a clear way to book a call.
alt: An OPEN sign hanging in a shop window, with the word SHOP printed on the glass, a plain statement of what the place is, which is the standard this article asks of a firm site.
caption: A shop window that says it is open and says it is a shop. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should an accounting firm remove from its website?
faqs.answer: Remove skylines, glass-tower photography, and lines like excellence or trusted partner that any firm could use. Remove capability grids with no outcome or boundary, and remove faces that are not your staff. Keep who does the work, the kind of company, and a way to book a call.

faqs.question: Is a longer accounting website better?
faqs.answer: Length is not the standard. Google's helpful-content guidance says Google does not have a preferred word count. A short site that names the person, the company type, and the next step is easier to keep true. Thin suburb pages and unnamed posts add volume without helping a founder.

faqs.question: What contact-page mistakes should go?
faqs.answer: A ten-field form, a chat tool dressed up as an accountant, and a phone number nobody answers. Ask for the company type, the ledger, and the question. Say how fast a person confirms, and say that the call is a fit check, not a finished return.

sources.title: How Long Do Users Stay on Web Pages?
Influencing your title links in search results

markdown:
The accounting firm website mistakes that confuse a founder are costume and volume. Cut the skyline and the word excellence. They reassure the people inside the firm and blur the view for a founder who needs a calm expert. Keep who does the work and for whom, and keep a clear way to book a call. A shorter site that tells the truth will do more than a long site performing taste.

Google's helpful-content guidance is plain about length. It asks whether you are writing to a word count because you heard Google prefers one, and it answers that Google does not. The same guidance treats trust as the important part of experience and expertise on topics that can affect financial stability. An accounting site sits in that group. Extra pages that repeat a mood do not create trust. Nielsen Norman Group found that people read only about a quarter of the text on pages they open, and often leave within 10 to 20 seconds. What you keep has to survive that skim.

## What to take off

Apply a cut list this week. If a block does not help a founder name the person, the kind of company, or the way to book, it is a candidate.

Skylines, glass lobbies, drones, and night cities. They photograph as "finance" and say nothing about who closes the books. A face and a sentence replace them.

Lines any firm can paste on. Excellence. Trusted partner. Bespoke solutions. Holistic. Synergy. Your growth journey. They soothe a partner reading the draft. They give a founder with a quiet ledger nothing to sort on.

A grid of capabilities with no outcome and no boundary. Advisory, compliance, strategy, each with the same two sentences. If you cannot say what they leave with and where the job stops, the item is not ready.

Awards as the first screen. A current, true mark can sit low. It cannot be the argument. A founder cannot hire a badge to explain a number.

Stock handshakes, rented diverse teams, and trading screens. If the face does not work at the firm, do not put it on the about page. A missing photo is more honest than a borrowed one.

A chat widget that implies an accountant is live. If the person on the other end cannot talk about the books, do not dress the tool as the expert. A button that books a call is plainer.

Invented statistics. "Average client saves 20 percent." If you cannot show the basis and you do not have permission, the number is a mistake, not proof. The Princeton GEO paper found that real statistics can raise visibility in generative answers. A made-up figure does the opposite the moment a careful founder checks.

## Why the costume survives

The skyline stays because the internal review is anxious. Partners want to look as established as the firms they admire, and those firms bought the same view. The review happens on a laptop, where excellence looks like confidence and a long page looks like substance.

The founder is not in that meeting. They are comparing two or three sites on a phone, looking for someone steady. A city they cannot hire is noise. An adjective they cannot test is noise. The partners' relief is not a test.

A second reason cuts get reversed: someone fills the space so the page does not look empty. Emptiness in the first screen is often the name finally being visible. Fill the space with the company type and the booking, not with a second slogan.

A third reason is search folklore. A vendor offers a page for every suburb and every synonym of accountant. Google's people-first questions warn against content made mainly to attract search, and against topics you do not really cover. Twenty thin location pages are that pattern. One page that says who you serve and where you are allowed to act is the version a founder can use, and the version you can keep true.

## What stays

Keep the person and the kind of company in the first view. "Mina Alvarez closes the books for owner-led studios." Add a boundary in the same breath. Who you do not take. Which entities. Which ledgers you know well, if that changes the fit.

Keep the booking, labeled the same way everywhere, with what happens after, how fast you really confirm, and what to have in mind. A short form or a calendar. A named role. A sentence that the call is a fit check, not a finished return.

Keep the people who do the work, including who signs if that is a different person from who closes the month. Keep one proof page only when you can tell a constraint and a decision without identifying a client or inventing a quote. Keep the fee shape if founders always ask, even when the dollar figure moves with the year.

Keep the address and a phone number only if they match reality. A dead number is a mistake. An email a person reads is enough when the relationship is mostly calls.

That set is a site. Homepage, services, people, proof if you have it, pricing if you can say the shape, and contact. You can add how a cleanup leads into a monthly close. You do not need a library of posts to look alive.

## Mistakes that look like content

A blog with no author, posted so the homepage looks current. If you write, write for the founder with the question, and name the accountant. Google asks who created the content. A nameless post fails. If you will not maintain it, do not start it.

Doorway pages that swap the suburb and keep the paragraph. Google's title-link guidance warns that boilerplate and inaccurate titles get replaced or ignored. Write one clear page instead of thirty echoes.

A brochure PDF that is the real pitch. Put the pitch on the site, where a person can update it without emailing a file. A download is a lobby.

Fake client quotations. You do not get to write the sentence and attribute it to "a SaaS founder." If you lack permission, skip the quote. The decision on a proof page is stronger than praise you authored.

Promises about tax outcomes. "We always lower the bill." Say you will explain the position and file what is supportable. That is the sentence you can keep, and it is the calm one.

Keyword lines in the footer. A city repeated under every synonym is a confession that the headings were unclear. Fix the headings. Google's title advice is to make each title distinct and descriptive, not to hide a keyword list where a founder might still read it and lose confidence.

Jokes about shoeboxes. Some founders are behind. Mocking them is the opposite of the expert they came to find. Describe the cleanup as a phase with a checkpoint.

## A shorter site is a site you can maintain

Every block has to change when a person leaves, a fee shape changes, or you stop taking a kind of company. Short sites get those edits. Long sites keep offering a call with someone who is gone.

Give one person the cut. A committee will restore excellence because deleting it feels rude. The standard is the founder. Read each block and ask what decision it changes. If the answer is none, cut it.

Google's note that there is no preferred word count is permission to stop padding. It is not permission to be vague. "We help businesses thrive" is short and useless. "We close the month for owner-led studios and clinics" is short and usable.

When you are unsure, cut the adjective and keep the noun. Keep the name, the company type, the ledger, the call. Release excellence, bespoke, and partner. The page will sound more like a firm that does the work.

## How to review the cuts

View the homepage on a phone and mark costume, then mark anything a stranger cannot act on. What remains should be the person, the company type, and the booking.

Show that screen to someone for ten seconds. Ask who does the work, for whom, and how they would book. If they mention the skyline, you did not cut enough. If they name a person and a company type, stop adding sections.

Check the title element on each page. "Monthly books for owner-led companies" beats "Services | Excellence." Distinct titles help a founder tell your pages apart, which is also what Google's title-link guidance is for.

Look at the contact form last. Cuts elsewhere do not help if the ask is still ten fields. The call is the point of the shorter site. Make it the easiest true thing on the page.

## What not to cut

Do not cut the boundary to sound welcoming. A false welcome creates the wrong call. Do not cut who signs. Do not cut the sentence that the first conversation is a fit check, not a filed return. Do not cut the kind of company in order to look bigger.

Do not cut readability when you remove a dark photograph. Reset the type so it still reads on a plain background. W3C's WCAG overview is the standard to keep: the page has to stay perceivable and operable. Gray text on a pale field is a new mistake.

Do not cut the true speed. If you confirm the next business day, say so.

After an accounting site tells the truth, it is worth seeing the same discipline on a different professional homepage, where the buyer is judging taste and the failure is a fullscreen render with no words. Read [what an architecture studio homepage has to prove](/blog/what-the-homepage-has-to-prove-for-an-architecture-studio). The proof there is built work with the constraint named, and the ask is a project conversation.
